newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Firms interested in Bosnia infrastructure but wary.
newsitem.headline: Firms interested in Bosnia infrastructure but wary.

text.p: International companies are interested in competing for infrastructure rebuilding contracts in Bosnia and Herzegovina but political uncertainty in the wake of its 43-month war means they are treading cautiously, Bosnia's minister of transport and communications, Rasim Gacanovic, said.

"There's really huge interest from foreign companies but people are waiting for a more stable political situation before they start with projects," he said in an interview on Tuesday after delivering a speech to an infrastructure conference.
Gacanovic said companies from Germany, Benelux, Italy, the U.S. and Japan had expressed interest in a range of projects.
"The main projects are those of reinstatement of road infrastructure," said Gacanovic, speaking through an interpreter.
"Then comes building air transport and somewhat less than that (in financial terms) for rail," he said.
Bosnia was facing a huge problem with years of bitter war savaging the country's infrastructure to the tune of $300 billion, the minister said.
"We've identified projects worth in the region of $70 billion and the United Nations has made an estimate that we need $5.2 billion in the next three years," he said.
He told the European market for Infrastructural Projects conference that the urgent need in air transport was for a trade hub to either Frankfurt or Amsterdam.
Cargo was particularly important for the transport of educational and training computers. "At the moment it's rather dangerous to transport that sort of thing by road," he said.

"We're interested in opening up one of our airports as an international airport for cargo. In my opinion this should be Tuzla," Gacanovic said, adding that any rebuilding would require the full range of airport equipment including air traffic control and other electronics.
But he acknowledged that, in the wake of the first elections in Bosnia since the war, international investment and further stability were inextricably linked.
"The best sign that stability has returned is when investments start in Bosnia and Herzegovina," he said. -- Keiron Henderson, Amsterdam Newsroom +31 20 504 5000
